claim: Human immune system (HIS) mice constructed in various ways are widely used for investigations of human immune responses to pathogens, transplants, and immunotherapies.
source: Human immune system (HIS) mice constructed in various ways are widely used for investigations of human immune responses to pathogens, transplants, and immunotherapies.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific practice in the field, representing common knowledge about HIS mouse models.

claim: In HIS mice that generate T cells de novo from hematopoietic progenitors, T cell-dependent multisystem autoimmune disease occurs.
source: In HIS mice that generate T cells de novo from hematopoietic progenitors, T cell-dependent multisystem autoimmune disease occurs, most rapidly when the human T cells develop in the native NOD.Cg- Prkdcscid Il2rgtm1Wjl (NSG) mouse thymus, where negative selection is abnormal.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' previous work and data presented in the manuscript showing disease development in these models.

claim: Disease develops most rapidly when human T cells develop in the native NSG mouse thymus, where negative selection is abnormal.
source: In HIS mice that generate T cells de novo from hematopoietic progenitors, T cell-dependent multisystem autoimmune disease occurs, most rapidly when the human T cells develop in the native NOD.Cg- Prkdcscid Il2rgtm1Wjl (NSG) mouse thymus, where negative selection is abnormal.
evidence: This is supported by comparative data between Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu mice showing faster disease onset in Mu/Hu mice and previous findings on abnormal negative selection.

claim: Disease develops very late when human T cells develop in human fetal thymus grafts, where robust negative selection is observed.
source: Disease develops very late when human T cells develop in human fetal thymus grafts, where robust negative selection is observed.
evidence: This is supported by data comparing disease onset timing between Hu/Hu and Mu/Hu mice and previous characterization of negative selection in human thymus grafts.

claim: PD-1+CD4+ peripheral (Tph) helper-like and follicular (Tfh) helper-like T cells developing in HIS mice can induce autoimmune disease.
source: We demonstrate here that PD-1+CD4+ peripheral (Tph) helper-like and follicular (Tfh) helper-like T cells developing in HIS mice can induce autoimmune disease.
evidence: This is demonstrated by adoptive transfer experiments showing that isolated Tfh and Tph cells can induce disease in recipient mice.

claim: Tfh-like cells were more prominent in HIS mice with a mouse thymus compared to those with a human thymus.
source: Tfh-like cells were more prominent in HIS mice with a mouse thymus, in which the highest levels of IgG were detected in plasma, compared to those with a human thymus.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2 showing higher percentages and numbers of Tfh-like cells in Mu/Hu mice.

claim: The highest levels of IgG were detected in plasma of HIS mice with a mouse thymus.
source: Tfh-like cells were more prominent in HIS mice with a mouse thymus, in which the highest levels of IgG were detected in plasma, compared to those with a human thymus.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 3B showing significantly higher IgG levels in Mu/Hu mice.

claim: Circulating IgG and IgM antibodies were autoreactive to multiple mouse antigens.
source: While circulating IgG and IgM antibodies were autoreactive to multiple mouse antigens, in vivo depletion of B cells and antibodies did not delay the development of autoimmune disease.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining of mouse tissues with HIS mouse sera (Figure 5A, Table 1) and ELISA assays for specific antigens (Figure 5C, E).

claim: In vivo depletion of B cells and antibodies did not delay the development of autoimmune disease.
source: While circulating IgG and IgM antibodies were autoreactive to multiple mouse antigens, in vivo depletion of B cells and antibodies did not delay the development of autoimmune disease.
evidence: This is demonstrated by rituximab treatment experiments (Figure 6) showing no delay or even acceleration of disease despite B cell depletion.

claim: Adoptive transfer of enriched Tfh- or Tph-like cells induced disease and autoimmunity-associated B cell phenotypes in recipient mice containing autologous human APCs without T cells.
source: Conversely, adoptive transfer of enriched Tfh- or Tph-like cells induced disease and autoimmunity-associated B cell phenotypes in recipient mice containing autologous human APCs without T cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by adoptive transfer experiments (Figures 7-8) showing disease development and increased CD11c+ B cells in recipients.

claim: Tfh/Tph cells from mice with a human thymus expanded and induced disease more rapidly than those originating in a murine thymus.
source: Tfh/Tph cells from mice with a human thymus expanded and induced disease more rapidly than those originating in a murine thymus, implicating HLA-restricted T cell-APC interactions in this process.
evidence: This is shown in adoptive transfer experiments (Figures 7-8) where Hu/Hu-derived T cells expanded faster and induced earlier disease than Mu/Hu-derived T cells.

claim: HLA-restricted T cell-APC interactions are implicated in the disease process.
source: Tfh/Tph cells from mice with a human thymus expanded and induced disease more rapidly than those originating in a murine thymus, implicating HLA-restricted T cell-APC interactions in this process.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential expansion and disease induction by Hu/Hu vs Mu/Hu T cells in the context of autologous human APCs.

claim: Tfh, Tph, autoantibodies, and lymphopenia-induced proliferation (LIP) have all been implicated in various forms of human autoimmune disease.
source: Since Tfh, Tph, autoantibodies, and lymphopenia-induced proliferation (LIP) have all been implicated in various forms of human autoimmune disease, the observations here provide a platform for the further dissection of human autoimmune disease mechanisms and therapies.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the autoimmune disease field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Human T cells developing de novo in the NSG mouse thymus do not undergo normal negative selection for self-antigens and lack normal thymocyte diversity.
source: However, we recently demonstrated that human T cells developing de novo in the NSG mouse thymus do not undergo normal negative selection for self-antigens and lack normal thymocyte diversity.
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous publication (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021).

claim: The thymus does not develop normal structure and contains a paucity of medullary epithelial cells in NSG mice.
source: We further showed that the thymus does not develop normal structure and contains a paucity of medullary epithelial cells.
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous publication (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021).

claim: T cells developing in the NSG mouse thymus induce a multiorgan disease characterized by human immune cell infiltrates in multiple organs, usually within 5–8 months after transplantation.
source: These T cells induce a multiorgan disease characterized by human immune cell infiltrates in multiple organs, usually within 5–8 months after transplantation (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous work cited and consistent with observations in the current study.

claim: Following transplantation of an autologous or partially HLA-matched human fetal thymus graft, the developing thymocytes undergo negative selection for self-antigens.
source: Following transplantation of an autologous or partially HLA-matched (to intravenously administered fetal CD34+ cells) human fetal thymus graft, the developing thymocytes undergo negative selection for self-antigens (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021), reflecting the presence of both human and murine (Kalscheuer et al., 2012) APCs in the thymus graft and the presence of a normal human cortico-medullary thymic structure (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous publications showing negative selection in human thymus grafts.

claim: Both human and murine APCs are present in the human thymus graft.
source: Following transplantation of an autologous or partially HLA-matched (to intravenously administered fetal CD34+ cells) human fetal thymus graft, the developing thymocytes undergo negative selection for self-antigens (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021), reflecting the presence of both human and murine (Kalscheuer et al., 2012) APCs in the thymus graft and the presence of a normal human cortico-medullary thymic structure (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by previous work (Kalscheuer et al., 2012) demonstrating murine APC presence in human thymus grafts.

claim: T cells developing in a human thymus graft eventually cause autoimmune disease, but with a significant delay if the native murine thymus has been removed.
source: T cells developing in a human thymus graft eventually cause autoimmune disease, but with a significant delay if the native murine thymus has been removed (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous work comparing disease onset in thymectomized vs non-thymectomized recipients.

claim: The slowly evolving autoimmune disease induced by T cells developing de novo in human thymus grafts is independent of direct recognition of murine antigens.
source: The slowly evolving autoimmune disease induced by T cells developing de novo in human thymus grafts is independent of direct recognition of murine antigens, as it develops with similar velocity in NSG mice expressing murine MHC and those completely lacking murine Class I and Class II MHC antigens (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in MHC-deficient mice showing similar disease kinetics.

claim: T cells from Hu/Hu and Mu/Hu mice showed proliferation to autologous human DCs.
source: As shown in Figure 1A and B, T cells from Hu/Hu and Mu/Hu mice showed proliferation to autologous human DCs that was not significantly augmented by pulsing of human DCs with murine antigens.
evidence: This is demonstrated by CFSE dilution assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: Proliferation of both CD4 and CD8 T cells to NSG mouse DCs was greater in Mu/Hu mice than in three of four Hu/Hu mice.
source: However, proliferation of both CD4 and CD8 T cells to NSG mouse DCs was greater in Mu/Hu mice than in three of four Hu/Hu mice, which showed little, if any, direct proliferation to murine antigens.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B comparing proliferation responses between groups.

claim: Proliferation of Mu/Hu CD4+ T cells to murine DCs was significantly greater than proliferation in the absence of DCs.
source: Proliferation of Mu/Hu CD4+ T cells to murine DCs was significantly greater than proliferation in the absence of DCs, in contrast to Hu/Hu CD4 cells, suggesting a lack of tolerance to NSG antigens only in Mu/Hu CD4+ T cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis of proliferation data in Figure 1B.

claim: Mu/Hu CD4+ T cells lack tolerance to NSG antigens.
source: Proliferation of Mu/Hu CD4+ T cells to murine DCs was significantly greater than proliferation in the absence of DCs, in contrast to Hu/Hu CD4 cells, suggesting a lack of tolerance to NSG antigens only in Mu/Hu CD4+ T cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential proliferation responses to murine DCs between Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu T cells.

claim: This observation is consistent with the lack of cortico-medullary structure or normal negative selection in the native murine thymi.
source: This observation is consistent with the lack of cortico-medullary structure or normal negative selection in the native murine thymi (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021).
evidence: This connects the proliferation data to previous structural and functional characterization of the murine thymus.

claim: CD3+ T cells were detected in peripheral blood around 12 weeks after transplantation.
source: CD3+ T cells were detected in peripheral blood around 12 weeks after transplantation (data not shown), as we previously reported (Kalscheuer et al., 2012; Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021; Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as an observation consistent with previous reports.

claim: Circulating Tph-like cells were detected at 13 weeks post-transplantation in both Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu groups.
source: Circulating Tph-like cells were detected at 13 weeks post-transplantation in both groups.
evidence: This is shown in the longitudinal flow cytometry data in Figure 2C.

claim: The frequency and absolute numbers of Tph-like cells in blood of Mu/Hu mice tended to be greater than those in Hu/Hu mice.
source: The frequency and absolute numbers of Tph-like cells in blood of Mu/Hu mice tended to be greater than those in Hu/Hu mice and the difference in percentages achieved statistical significance across multiple time points (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by longitudinal flow cytometry data with statistical analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: Circulating Tfh-like cells appeared at 13 weeks post-transplantation in Mu/Hu mice.
source: Circulating Tfh-like cells appeared at 13 weeks post-transplantation in Mu/Hu mice (Figure 2D), increased progressively over time and were significantly more abundant in this group than in Hu/Hu mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in the longitudinal flow cytometry data in Figure 2D.

claim: Circulating Tfh-like cells were significantly more abundant in Mu/Hu mice than in Hu/Hu mice.
source: Circulating Tfh-like cells appeared at 13 weeks post-transplantation in Mu/Hu mice (Figure 2D), increased progressively over time and were significantly more abundant in this group than in Hu/Hu mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical comparison of longitudinal data in Figure 2D.

claim: No significant differences in Tph-like cell frequency and absolute numbers were detected between Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu groups in spleens.
source: While no significant differences in Tph-like cell frequency and absolute numbers were detected between the two groups (Figure 2F), percentages of Tfh-like cells were significantly greater in spleens of Mu/Hu compared to Hu/Hu mice (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is shown by splenic flow cytometry analysis in Figure 2F.

claim: Percentages of Tfh-like cells were significantly greater in spleens of Mu/Hu compared to Hu/Hu mice.
source: While no significant differences in Tph-like cell frequency and absolute numbers were detected between the two groups (Figure 2F), percentages of Tfh-like cells were significantly greater in spleens of Mu/Hu compared to Hu/Hu mice (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by splenic flow cytometry analysis with statistical comparison in Figure 2G.

claim: The numbers of both Tph-like and Tfh-like cells increased over time in both HIS mouse groups.
source: The numbers of both Tph-like and Tfh-like cells increased over time in both HIS mouse groups and staining for Ki67 revealed high proliferative rates for both cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by longitudinal analysis in Figure 2 and Ki67 staining in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Staining for Ki67 revealed high proliferative rates for both Tph-like and Tfh-like cell types.
source: The numbers of both Tph-like and Tfh-like cells increased over time in both HIS mouse groups and staining for Ki67 revealed high proliferative rates for both cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Ki67 flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tph-like and Tfh-like cells in HIS mice expressed higher levels of ICOS compared to control CD45RA+ T cells.
source: These cells expressed higher levels of ICOS (Figure 2H) and, upon phorbol myristic acid (PMA)/ionomycin stimulation, secreted more IL-21 (Figure 2I) compared to control, CD45RA+ T cells, consistent with helper function and with their role in humans.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis of ICOS expression in Figure 2H.

claim: Upon PMA/ionomycin stimulation, Tph-like and Tfh-like cells secreted more IL-21 compared to control CD45RA+ T cells.
source: These cells expressed higher levels of ICOS (Figure 2H) and, upon phorbol myristic acid (PMA)/ionomycin stimulation, secreted more IL-21 (Figure 2I) compared to control, CD45RA+ T cells, consistent with helper function and with their role in humans.
evidence: This is demonstrated by intracellular cytokine staining in Figure 2I.

claim: The majority of Tfh-like and Tph-like cells in Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu mice expressed ICOS.
source: The majority of Tfh-like and Tph-like cells in Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu mice expressed ICOS, though the percentage of ICOS+ cells was significantly higher in Mu/Hu Tfh-like and Tph-like cells compared to their Hu/Hu counterparts (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry analysis in Figure 2J.

claim: The percentage of ICOS+ cells was significantly higher in Mu/Hu Tfh-like and Tph-like cells compared to their Hu/Hu counterparts.
source: The majority of Tfh-like and Tph-like cells in Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu mice expressed ICOS, though the percentage of ICOS+ cells was significantly higher in Mu/Hu Tfh-like and Tph-like cells compared to their Hu/Hu counterparts (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical comparison of ICOS expression in Figure 2J.

claim: Approximately 10% of Tfh-like and Tph-like cells in both Hu/Hu and Mu/Hu groups were FOXP3+.
source: Approximately 10% of Tfh-like and Tph-like cells in both Hu/Hu and Mu/Hu groups were FOXP3+, with the highest proportion observed in Hu/Hu Tph-like cells (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry analysis of FOXP3 expression in Figure 2K.

claim: Overall B cell reconstitution was similar between Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu mice.
source: While overall B cell reconstitution (Figure 3A) and serum IgM concentration was similar between Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu mice, serum IgG levels were significantly greater in Mu/Hu mice (Figure 3B), suggesting increased B cell differentiation and IgG class switching.
evidence: This is shown by longitudinal flow cytometry data in Figure 3A.

claim: Serum IgM concentration was similar between Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu mice.
source: While overall B cell reconstitution (Figure 3A) and serum IgM concentration was similar between Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu mice, serum IgG levels were significantly greater in Mu/Hu mice (Figure 3B), suggesting increased B cell differentiation and IgG class switching.
evidence: This is shown by ELISA data in Figure 3B.

claim: Serum IgG levels were significantly greater in Mu/Hu mice compared to Hu/Hu mice.
source: While overall B cell reconstitution (Figure 3A) and serum IgM concentration was similar between Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu mice, serum IgG levels were significantly greater in Mu/Hu mice (Figure 3B), suggesting increased B cell differentiation and IgG class switching.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data with statistical comparison in Figure 3B.

claim: The increased IgG in Mu/Hu mice suggests increased B cell differentiation and IgG class switching.
source: While overall B cell reconstitution (Figure 3A) and serum IgM concentration was similar between Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu mice, serum IgG levels were significantly greater in Mu/Hu mice (Figure 3B), suggesting increased B cell differentiation and IgG class switching.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the IgG data based on known B cell biology.

claim: Helper cells from both Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu mice induced plasmablast formation in vitro.
source: Helper cells from both Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu mice induced plasmablast formation and this activity was greater at later (>20 weeks) than earlier (<20 weeks) times post-transplant.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro T-B cell co-culture assays shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Helper cell activity for inducing plasmablast formation was greater at later (>20 weeks) than earlier (<20 weeks) times post-transplant.
source: Helper cells from both Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu mice induced plasmablast formation and this activity was greater at later (>20 weeks) than earlier (<20 weeks) times post-transplant.
evidence: This is shown by comparing plasmablast differentiation at different time points in Figure 3D.

claim: Tfh-like cells from Hu/Hu mice demonstrated greater B cell helper function than those from Mu/Hu mice, particularly in the later time period.
source: However, Tfh-like cells from Hu/Hu mice demonstrated greater B cell helper function than those from Mu/Hu mice, particularly in the later time period.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing plasmablast induction between groups in Figure 3D.

claim: T-B cell interactions are more effective for T cells generated in a human thymus that is isogenic to the B cells than for those generated in a xenogeneic murine thymus.
source: A similar trend was seen for Tph-like cells (Figure 3D), indicating that T-B cell interactions are more effective for T cells generated in a human thymus that is isogenic to the B cells than for those generated in a xenogeneic murine thymus, and consistent with previous literature (Lang et al., 2013; Danner et al., 2011; Suzuki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential helper function data and supported by previous literature.

claim: Human CXCL13 was detected in both Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu groups.
source: While human CXCL13 was detected in both groups and did not correlate with the number of splenic Tfh or Tph cells (data not shown), the levels tended to be higher in Mu/Hu compared to Hu/Hu mice (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown by ELISA data in Figure 3E.

claim: CXCL13 levels did not correlate with the number of splenic Tfh or Tph cells.
source: While human CXCL13 was detected in both groups and did not correlate with the number of splenic Tfh or Tph cells (data not shown), the levels tended to be higher in Mu/Hu compared to Hu/Hu mice (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated as a negative correlation finding.

claim: CXCL13 levels tended to be higher in Mu/Hu compared to Hu/Hu mice.
source: While human CXCL13 was detected in both groups and did not correlate with the number of splenic Tfh or Tph cells (data not shown), the levels tended to be higher in Mu/Hu compared to Hu/Hu mice (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown by ELISA data in Figure 3E, though the difference did not reach statistical significance.

claim: Spleens showed a semiorganized structure with distinct B and T cell localization and well-defined follicles up to 30 weeks post-transplant in both groups.
source: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining revealed a semiorganized splenic structure, with distinct B and T cell localization and well-defined follicles up to 30 weeks post-transplant in both groups.
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: After 30 weeks, spleens showed fewer B cell follicles and appeared disorganized.
source: However, after 30 weeks, spleens showed fewer B cell follicles and appeared disorganized (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is shown by histological analysis and quantification in Figure 4B and C.

claim: There were no significant differences in the number or total area of splenic follicles between Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu mice.
source: Despite the increased number of Tfh-like cells in the spleens of Mu/Hu mice, there were no significant differences in the number or total area of splenic follicles between Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by quantitative analysis of follicular areas in Figure 4B.

claim: Serum from Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu mice contained IgM antibodies that were reactive to multiple murine tissues.
source: As shown in Figure 5A and Table 1, serum from Mu/Hu and Hu/Hu mice contained IgM antibodies that were reactive to multiple murine tissues.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining of mouse tissues in Figure 5A and Table 1.

claim: Several Mu/Hu mice contained IgG antibodies with broad reactivity to multiple murine tissues.
source: Several Mu/Hu mice also contained IgG antibodies with broad reactivity to multiple murine tissues.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 documenting tissue reactivity patterns.

claim: IgM in sera from HIS mice was reactive to LPS, insulin, and dsDNA.
source: IgM in sera from HIS mice was reactive to LPS, insulin, and dsDNA, and these levels increased over time irrespective of the thymus type (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA assays in Figure 5C.

claim: IgM reactivity to LPS, insulin, and dsDNA increased over time irrespective of the thymus type.
source: IgM in sera from HIS mice was reactive to LPS, insulin, and dsDNA, and these levels increased over time irrespective of the thymus type (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown by longitudinal ELISA data in Figure 5C.

claim: IgG against LPS, insulin, and dsDNA increased over time in both groups.
source: IgG against these antigens also increased over time in both groups (Figure 5E), even though total IgG levels tended to be higher in Mu/Hu than Hu/Hu mice (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by longitudinal ELISA data in Figure 5E.

claim: The sum of IgM reactivities to dsDNA, insulin, and LPS was >100% of total serum IgM for three Mu/Hu mice, consistent with polyreactivity.
source: To assess the possibility that IgM autoantibodies might be polyreactive, we compared the sum of IgM concentrations reacting to dsDNA, insulin, and LPS to total serum IgM concentrations and observed that the sum of these reactivities was >100% for three Mu/Hu mice (Figure 5F), consistent with polyreactivity of individual B cells in these mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis in Figure 5F showing that summed reactivities exceed total IgM.

claim: Mu/Hu mice showed increased proportions of activated or age-associated B cells (IgD⁻CD27+CD11c+) compared to Hu/Hu mice.
source: These studies revealed increased proportions of activated or age-associated B cells (IgD⁻CD27+CD11c+) and atypical B cells (IgD⁻CD27⁻CD11c+) in Mu/Hu mice compared to those from Hu/Hu mice (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry analysis in Figure 5G.

claim: Mu/Hu mice showed increased proportions of atypical B cells (IgD⁻CD27⁻CD11c+) compared to Hu/Hu mice.
source: These studies revealed increased proportions of activated or age-associated B cells (IgD⁻CD27+CD11c+) and atypical B cells (IgD⁻CD27⁻CD11c+) in Mu/Hu mice compared to those from Hu/Hu mice (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry analysis in Figure 5G.

claim: Rituximab treatment successfully depleted B cells from the circulation and eliminated serum IgM.
source: As shown in Figure 6B, this treatment successfully depleted B cells from the circulation and eliminated serum IgM.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry and ELISA data in Figure 6B.

claim: Immunofluorescent analysis of serum IgM from rituximab-treated mice showed an absence of autoreactive IgM.
source: Immunofluorescent analysis of serum IgM from rituximab-treated mice showed an absence of autoreactive IgM (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence staining in Figure 6C.

claim: B cell depletion with rituximab did not prevent or delay disease development when started at 20 weeks.
source: However, B cell depletion with this method did not prevent or even delay disease development (Figure 6D), suggesting a minor, if any, role for antibodies in disease progression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival curve analysis in Figure 6D.

claim: Starting rituximab treatment 1 week post-transplant significantly accelerated disease development.
source: As shown in Figure 6E, starting rituximab treatment 1 week post-transplant and continuing through the post-transplant course also failed to delay or reduce the development of disease and, surprisingly, significantly accelerated its development.
evidence: This is demonstrated by survival curve analysis in Figure 6E.

claim: Antibodies were not required for disease development.
source: From these results, we concluded that antibodies were not required for disease development.
evidence: This is concluded from the rituximab depletion experiments showing disease development despite B cell and antibody depletion.

claim: Both Tfh-like and Tph-like cells originating in Hu/Hu mice expanded faster and to a greater extent than those originating in Mu/Hu mice in adoptive transfer recipients.
source: As shown in Figure 7C and D, both Tfh-like and Tph-like cells originating in Hu/Hu mice expanded faster and to a greater extent than those originating in Mu/Hu mice, achieving higher circulating levels.
evidence: This is demonstrated by longitudinal flow cytometry analysis in adoptive recipients shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: Recipients of Tfh-like cells from Hu/Hu mice contained high numbers of circulating Tph-like and much lower numbers of Tfh-like cells.
source: Recipients of Tfh-like cells from Hu/Hu mice contained high numbers of circulating Tph-like and much lower numbers of Tfh-like cells (Figure 7E and F), suggesting that Tfh-like cells might have lost CXCR5 expression or that Tph-like contaminants expanded preferentially.
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry analysis of adoptive recipients in Figure 7E and F.

claim: Tfh-like cells might have lost CXCR5 expression or Tph-like contaminants expanded preferentially in adoptive recipients.
source: Recipients of Tfh-like cells from Hu/Hu mice contained high numbers of circulating Tph-like and much lower numbers of Tfh-like cells (Figure 7E and F), suggesting that Tfh-like cells might have lost CXCR5 expression or that Tph-like contaminants expanded preferentially.
evidence: This is speculated based on the phenotypic shift observed in adoptive recipients.

claim: By 5 weeks following adoptive transfer, the blood of recipients of Tfh and Tph cells from Hu/Hu mice exhibited increased levels of CD11c+ B cells compared to recipients of T cells from Mu/Hu mice.
source: By 5 weeks following adoptive transfer, the blood of recipients of Tfh and Tph cells from Hu/Hu mice exhibited increased levels of CD11c+ B cells, an effector B cell population associated with aging, infection, and human autoimmune diseases, compared to recipients of T cells from Mu/Hu mice (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis in Figure 8C.

claim: CD11c+ B cells are an effector B cell population associated with aging, infection, and human autoimmune diseases.
source: By 5 weeks following adoptive transfer, the blood of recipients of Tfh and Tph cells from Hu/Hu mice exhibited increased levels of CD11c+ B cells, an effector B cell population associated with aging, infection, and human autoimmune diseases, compared to recipients of T cells from Mu/Hu mice (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CD11c+ B cells.

claim: The increase in CD11c+ B cells largely reflected an increase in the percentage of atypical B cells (IgD⁻CD27⁻CD11c+, DN2) in the recipients of Hu/Hu T cells.
source: This difference largely reflected an increase in the percentage of atypical B cells (IgD⁻CD27⁻CD11c+, DN2) in the recipients of Hu/Hu T cells.
evidence: This is shown by detailed B cell subset analysis in Figure 8C.

claim: Both activated or age-associated B cells and atypical B cells were significantly increased in the spleens of recipients of Hu/Hu Tph and Tfh cells compared to recipients of Mu/Hu Tph and Tfh cells.
source: Both activated or age-associated B cells (IgD⁻CD27+CD11c+) and atypical B cells (IgD⁻CD27⁻CD11c+) were significantly increased in the spleens of recipients of Hu/Hu Tph and Tfh cells compared to recipients of Mu/Hu Tph and Tfh cells 9 weeks following adoptive transfer (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by splenic flow cytometry analysis in Figure 8C.

claim: Recipients of Tfh-like or Tph-like cells from Hu/Hu mice had higher levels of IgM and IgG antibodies compared to recipients of Tfh-like or Tph-like cells from Mu/Hu mice.
source: Recipients of Tfh-like or Tph-like cells from Hu/Hu mice had higher levels of IgM and IgG antibodies compared to recipients of Tfh-like or Tph-like cells from Mu/Hu mice and the APC-only controls contained IgM at low levels and undetectable levels of IgG (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ELISA data in Figure 8D.

claim: APC-only controls contained IgM at low levels and undetectable levels of IgG.
source: Recipients of Tfh-like or Tph-like cells from Hu/Hu mice had higher levels of IgM and IgG antibodies compared to recipients of Tfh-like or Tph-like cells from Mu/Hu mice and the APC-only controls contained IgM at low levels and undetectable levels of IgG (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is shown by ELISA data in Figure 8D.

claim: Tfh-like and Tph-like cells play a role in inducing both IgM and IgG antibodies in HIS mice.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate a role for Tfh-like and Tph-like cells in inducing both IgM and IgG antibodies in HIS mice and show that T cells from Hu/Hu mice provide help for autologous B cell antibody responses more effectively than those from Mu/Hu mice.
evidence: This is concluded from the adoptive transfer experiments showing antibody production dependent on T cell transfer.

claim: T cells from Hu/Hu mice provide help for autologous B cell antibody responses more effectively than those from Mu/Hu mice.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate a role for Tfh-like and Tph-like cells in inducing both IgM and IgG antibodies in HIS mice and show that T cells from Hu/Hu mice provide help for autologous B cell antibody responses more effectively than those from Mu/Hu mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing antibody levels and B cell phenotypes in recipients of Hu/Hu vs Mu/Hu T cells.

claim: Adoptive recipients of Tfh-like and Tph-like cells from Hu/Hu mice lost weight beginning at 7 and 9 weeks, respectively.
source: Adoptive recipients of Tfh-like and Tph-like cells from Hu/Hu mice lost weight beginning at 7 and 9 weeks, respectively, whereas the recipients of Mu/Hu T cells did not show obvious weight loss (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is shown by longitudinal weight measurements in Figure 8E.

claim: Recipients of Mu/Hu T cells did not show obvious weight loss.
source: Adoptive recipients of Tfh-like and Tph-like cells from Hu/Hu mice lost weight beginning at 7 and 9 weeks, respectively, whereas the recipients of Mu/Hu T cells did not show obvious weight loss (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is shown by longitudinal weight measurements in Figure 8E.

claim: Clinical disease was more apparent in recipients of Hu/Hu T cells, with the most rapid onset in recipients of Hu/Hu Tfh-like cells.
source: Clinical disease was also more apparent in recipients of Hu/Hu T cells, with the most rapid onset in recipients of Hu/Hu Tfh-like cells.
evidence: This is shown by disease scoring and survival analysis in Figure 8F.

claim: Most recipients of Mu/Hu T cells did not develop clinically apparent disease during the follow-up period.
source: In contrast, most recipients of Mu/Hu T cells did not develop clinically apparent disease during the follow-up period (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is shown by survival curve analysis in Figure 8F.

claim: T cells developing in an autologous human thymus graft interact more effectively with peripheral B cells and other APCs, presumably reflecting thymic positive selection on the same HLA molecules as those in the peripheral APCs.
source: Together, our data suggest that T cells developing in an autologous human thymus graft interact more effectively with peripheral B cells and other APCs, presumably reflecting thymic positive selection on the same HLA molecules as those in the peripheral APCs, resulting in T cell expansion, increased CD11c expression on B cells, and eventually disease development.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential expansion and function of Hu/Hu vs Mu/Hu T cells in adoptive recipients.

claim: The lack of a functional C5 complement component may help explain the lack of pathogenicity of autoantibodies observed in the studies.
source: The lack of a functional C5 complement component, rendering membrane attack complex and C5a anaphylatoxin production impossible, may help to explain the lack of pathogenicity of autoantibodies observed in our studies and different results might be obtained in NSG recipients engineered to correct the C5 deficiency (Verma et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation based on known complement biology and the genetic deficiency in NSG mice.

claim: The acceleration of disease in animals depleted of B cells from the beginning of the post-transplant period suggests that B cells may play a predominantly regulatory role in this model.
source: In fact, the acceleration of disease in animals depleted of B cells from the beginning of the post-transplant period suggests that B cells may play a predominantly regulatory role in this model.
evidence: This is inferred from the early rituximab treatment experiment showing accelerated disease.

claim: Adoptive recipients of Tph-like and Tfh-like cells from Hu/Hu mice demonstrated an increase in CD11c+ B cells compared to counterparts receiving T cells from Mu/Hu mice.
source: Nevertheless, it is noteworthy that adoptive recipients of Tph-like and Tfh-like cells from Hu/Hu mice demonstrated an increase (compared to counterparts receiving T cells from Mu/Hu mice) in CD11c+ B cells, an effector B cell population otherwise known as age-associated B cells that is increased in association with human autoimmune diseases (Mouat et al., 2022; Karnell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 8C and supported by literature on CD11c+ B cells in autoimmunity.

claim: CD11c+ B cells are otherwise known as age-associated B cells that are increased in association with human autoimmune diseases.
source: Nevertheless, it is noteworthy that adoptive recipients of Tph-like and Tfh-like cells from Hu/Hu mice demonstrated an increase (compared to counterparts receiving T cells from Mu/Hu mice) in CD11c+ B cells, an effector B cell population otherwise known as age-associated B cells that is increased in association with human autoimmune diseases (Mouat et al., 2022; Karnell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD11c+ B cells supported by citations.

claim: Tfh- and Tph-like cells from Hu/Hu mice have the capacity to induce the differentiation of CD11c+ B cells.
source: These data directly demonstrate the capacity of Tfh- and Tph-like cells from Hu/Hu, and to a lesser extent, from Mu/Hu mice, to induce the differentiation of this unique B cell subset.
evidence: This is concluded from the adoptive transfer experiments showing increased CD11c+ B cells in recipients.

claim: Adoptive transfer studies directly demonstrate the capacity of Tfh- and Tph-like cells generated in HIS mice to induce class-switched IgG-expressing and IgG-secreting B cells.
source: Our adoptive transfer studies also directly demonstrate the capacity of Tfh- and Tph-like cells generated in HIS mice to induce class-switched IgG-expressing and IgG-secreting B cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the antibody and B cell phenotype data from adoptive recipients in Figure 8.

claim: In vitro studies demonstrated effective help for differentiation of autologous B cells by T cells that differentiate in an autologous human thymus graft.
source: In vitro studies demonstrated effective help for differentiation of autologous B cells by T cells that differentiate in an autologous human thymus graft and less effective T-B interactions for T cells that differentiated in the xenogeneic murine thymus.
evidence: This is shown by the in vitro T-B cell co-culture assays in Figure 3D.

claim: T cells that differentiated in the xenogeneic murine thymus showed less effective T-B interactions.
source: In vitro studies demonstrated effective help for differentiation of autologous B cells by T cells that differentiate in an autologous human thymus graft and less effective T-B interactions for T cells that differentiated in the xenogeneic murine thymus.
evidence: This is shown by comparing plasmablast induction between Hu/Hu and Mu/Hu T cells in Figure 3D.

claim: Positive selection in an autologous thymus generates T cells that interact more effectively with autologous human APCs and B cells than T cells generated in a murine thymus lacking HLA molecules.
source: These results are consistent with the interpretation that positive selection in an autologous thymus generates T cells that interact more effectively with autologous human APCs and B cells than T cells generated in a murine thymus lacking HLA molecules.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential T-B cell interaction data and is consistent with known principles of MHC restriction.

claim: T cells have been shown to be essential for B cell maturation in HIS mice.
source: Indeed, T cells have been shown to be essential for B cell maturation in HIS mice (Lang et al., 2013) and increased IgG levels are detected in association with greater T cell reconstitution (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021; Lang et al., 2013; Brainard et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established by previous literature cited.

claim: Increased IgG levels are detected in association with greater T cell reconstitution in HIS mice.
source: Indeed, T cells have been shown to be essential for B cell maturation in HIS mice (Lang et al., 2013) and increased IgG levels are detected in association with greater T cell reconstitution (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021; Lang et al., 2013; Brainard et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple previous publications cited.

claim: Introduction of an HLA Class II molecule into the mouse has been reported to enhance human T-B cell interactions in HIS mice with a murine thymus.
source: Furthermore, introduction of an HLA Class II molecule into the mouse has been reported to enhance human T-B cell interactions in HIS mice with a murine thymus (Danner et al., 2011; Suzuki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established by previous literature cited.

claim: The failure to negatively select human autoreactive T cells in the murine thymus may explain the paradoxical increase in IgG and activated B cells in Mu/Hu mice despite improved T-B interactions in Hu/Hu mice.
source: However, we believe the failure to negatively select human autoreactive T cells in the murine thymus, as we have previously reported (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021), may provide an explanation for this paradox.
evidence: This is proposed as an explanation based on previous findings and current data.

claim: If human T cells developing in a murine thymus are not centrally tolerized to murine antigens presented by human APCs, they may react with human APCs loaded with murine antigens in a manner that resembles an alloresponse.
source: If human T cells developing in a murine thymus are not centrally tolerized to murine antigens presented by human APCs, they may be expected to react with human APCs loaded with murine antigens, including human B cells, in the periphery in a manner that resembles an alloresponse.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on principles of T cell tolerance and allorecognition.

claim: Alloresponses can activate B cells and induce polyclonal class-switched antibody responses that include autoantibodies.
source: Alloresponses can activate B cells and induce polyclonal class-switched antibody responses that include autoantibodies, as shown in MHC heterozygous (F1) mice receiving MHC homozygous parental T cells, eliciting a GVH response that manifests as autoimmunity with autoantibodies, referred to as 'lupus-like' GVHD (Soloviova et al., 2012; Tschetter et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to mouse GVHD models.

claim: Responses of Mu/Hu splenic CD4 T cells to mouse antigen-loaded human DCs were stronger than those of Hu/Hu splenic T cells.
source: Consistent with this possibility, responses of Mu/Hu splenic CD4 T cells to mouse antigen-loaded human DCs were stronger than those of Hu/Hu splenic T cells.
evidence: This is shown by the proliferation assay data in Figure 1.

claim: The increase in activated/age-associated and atypical B cells in Mu/Hu compared to Hu/Hu mice points to increased B cell activation in Mu/Hu mice.
source: Additionally, the increase in activated/age-associated (IgD-CD27+CD11c+) and atypical (IgD-CD27-CD11c+) B cells in Mu/Hu compared to Hu/Hu mice points to increased B cell activation in Mu/Hu mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the B cell phenotype data in Figure 5G.

claim: Lymphopenia-induced proliferation (LIP) of T cells entering the periphery is increased in Mu/Hu compared to Hu/Hu mice.
source: Additional studies indicate that lymphopenia-induced proliferation (LIP) of T cells entering the periphery is increased in Mu/Hu compared to Hu/Hu mice, in which thymopoiesis and peripheral T cell reconstitution is more robust, and that LIP plays a significant role in the development of disease (M Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., manuscript in preparation).
evidence: This refers to unpublished data from the authors.

claim: LIP plays a significant role in the development of disease in HIS mice.
source: Additional studies indicate that lymphopenia-induced proliferation (LIP) of T cells entering the periphery is increased in Mu/Hu compared to Hu/Hu mice, in which thymopoiesis and peripheral T cell reconstitution is more robust, and that LIP plays a significant role in the development of disease (M Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., manuscript in preparation).
evidence: This refers to unpublished data from the authors.

claim: Studies in mice have strongly implicated LIP in autoimmune disease development.
source: Consistently, studies in mice have strongly implicated LIP in autoimmune disease development (King et al., 2004; Le Campion et al., 2009; McPherson et al., 2009; Zhang and Bevan, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Adoptive transfer of Hu/Hu T cells led to more rapid expansion than that of Mu/Hu T cells.
source: Adoptive transfer of Hu/Hu T cells led to more rapid expansion than that of Mu/Hu T cells, suggesting that recognition of the same HLA antigens in the periphery as those mediating thymic positive selection optimizes LIP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the adoptive transfer experiments in Figure 7.

claim: Recognition of the same HLA antigens in the periphery as those mediating thymic positive selection optimizes LIP.
source: Adoptive transfer of Hu/Hu T cells led to more rapid expansion than that of Mu/Hu T cells, suggesting that recognition of the same HLA antigens in the periphery as those mediating thymic positive selection optimizes LIP.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential expansion of Hu/Hu vs Mu/Hu T cells in adoptive recipients.

claim: This increased LIP may account for the more rapid disease development in the recipients of Hu/Hu than Mu/Hu Tfh- and Tph-like cells.
source: This increased LIP may account for the more rapid disease development in the recipients of Hu/Hu than Mu/Hu Tfh- and Tph-like cells.
evidence: This is proposed as an explanation for the disease kinetics observed in adoptive recipients.

claim: Human peripheral APCs are absolutely required for survival, LIP, and effector differentiation of Hu/Hu T cells.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, we have previously demonstrated that human peripheral APCs are absolutely required for survival, LIP, and effector differentiation of Hu/Hu T cells (Onoe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous publication.

claim: Rapid LIP of human T cells is likely to be antigen-driven, as reported for murine T cells.
source: As reported for murine T cells (Min et al., 2005; Surh and Sprent, 2008), rapid LIP of human T cells is likely to be antigen-driven.
evidence: This is inferred based on established knowledge from mouse studies.

claim: Indirect presentation of murine antigens on human APCs is sufficient to drive disease.
source: Given that indirect presentation of murine antigens on human APCs is sufficient to drive disease (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021), we conclude that incomplete negative selection of indirectly xenoreactive mouse-specific T cells (possibly recognizing tissue-restricted antigens normally produced by murine thymic epithelial cells, which are absent in human thymus grafts) in a human thymus allows these T cells to recognize murine peptides presented on human APCs.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous work showing disease in MHC-deficient mice.

claim: Incomplete negative selection of indirectly xenoreactive mouse-specific T cells in a human thymus allows these T cells to recognize murine peptides presented on human APCs.
source: Given that indirect presentation of murine antigens on human APCs is sufficient to drive disease (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021), we conclude that incomplete negative selection of indirectly xenoreactive mouse-specific T cells (possibly recognizing tissue-restricted antigens normally produced by murine thymic epithelial cells, which are absent in human thymus grafts) in a human thymus allows these T cells to recognize murine peptides presented on human APCs.
evidence: This is concluded based on the disease development in Hu/Hu mice and known principles of thymic selection.

claim: This interpretation is consistent with in vitro findings of tolerance to murine antigens presented directly on murine DCs.
source: This interpretation is consistent with our in vitro findings of tolerance to murine antigens presented directly on murine DCs, since murine APCs are present in the human thymic medulla of Hu/Hu mice (Kalscheuer et al., 2012) and of weak but measurable reactivity to autologous DCs capable of presenting murine antigens indirectly.
evidence: This connects the proliferation assay data to the proposed mechanism and previous findings.

claim: Murine APCs are present in the human thymic medulla of Hu/Hu mice.
source: This interpretation is consistent with our in vitro findings of tolerance to murine antigens presented directly on murine DCs, since murine APCs are present in the human thymic medulla of Hu/Hu mice (Kalscheuer et al., 2012) and of weak but measurable reactivity to autologous DCs capable of presenting murine antigens indirectly.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited.

claim: Lack of tolerance to murine antigens in the primary Mu/Hu mice reflects the lack of medullary structure and of central tolerance in the native mouse thymus.
source: While lack of tolerance to murine antigens in the primary Mu/Hu mice reflects the lack of medullary structure and of central tolerance in the native mouse thymus (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021), the number of these T cells that expand in the periphery may be constrained by their positive selection on murine cortical epithelium and MHC, resulting in a more oligoclonal (compared to Hu/Hu mice) expansion of T cells recognizing murine peptides presented on human APCs expressing HLA.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous characterization of the murine thymus.

claim: The number of T cells that expand in the periphery of Mu/Hu mice may be constrained by their positive selection on murine cortical epithelium and MHC.
source: While lack of tolerance to murine antigens in the primary Mu/Hu mice reflects the lack of medullary structure and of central tolerance in the native mouse thymus (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021), the number of these T cells that expand in the periphery may be constrained by their positive selection on murine cortical epithelium and MHC, resulting in a more oligoclonal (compared to Hu/Hu mice) expansion of T cells recognizing murine peptides presented on human APCs expressing HLA.
evidence: This is proposed as an explanation for the differential expansion patterns.

claim: This situation is exacerbated by the markedly reduced diversity of the human TCR repertoire selected in the native murine thymus vs the human thymus graft.
source: This situation is exacerbated by the markedly reduced diversity of the human TCR repertoire selected in the native murine thymus vs the human thymus graft (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous TCR repertoire analysis.

claim: The extensive expansion of a smaller population of peripheral T cells in Mu/Hu compared to Hu/Hu mice may have resulted in exhaustion of Tfh- and Tph-like cells in Mu/Hu mice prior to the time of transfer.
source: The extensive expansion of a smaller population of peripheral T cells in Mu/Hu compared to Hu/Hu mice may have resulted in exhaustion of Tfh- and Tph-like cells in Mu/Hu mice prior to the time of transfer, delaying disease onset in adoptive recipients.
evidence: This is proposed as a possible explanation for the delayed disease in recipients of Mu/Hu T cells.

claim: Exhaustion has been reported for human T cells in HIS mice with GVHD and chronic HIV infection.
source: Exhaustion has been reported for human T cells in HIS mice with GVHD (Tary-Lehmann et al., 1994) and chronic HIV infection (Brainard et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established by previous literature cited.

claim: The observed inability of direct antigen presentation on murine cells to drive LIP or disease development likely reflects failed coreceptor, costimulatory, adhesive, and/or cytokine interactions between human T cells and murine cells.
source: The observed inability of direct antigen presentation on murine cells to drive LIP (Onoe et al., 2010) or disease development (Khosravi-Maharlooei et al., 2021), and hence dependence on antigen presentation on human APCs likely reflects failed coreceptor, costimulatory, adhesive, and/or cytokine interactions between human T cells and murine cells.
evidence: This is proposed as an explanation based on known requirements for T cell activation and previous findings.

claim: An additional possible contributor to accelerated autoimmune disease development in Mu/Hu compared to Hu/Hu mice may be inferior Treg function in the Mu/Hu group.
source: An additional possible contributor to accelerated autoimmune disease development in Mu/Hu compared to Hu/Hu mice may be inferior Treg function in the Mu/Hu group due to the incompatibility of the MHC of the murine thymic epithelium and the paucity of medullary epithelium responsible for positive selection of Tregs, resulting in a deficiency of Tregs that are capable of interacting with human APCs in the periphery or capable of recognizing murine antigens directly.
evidence: This is proposed as a possible contributing mechanism based on known Treg biology.

claim: This interpretation is consistent with the known role of Tregs in regulating Tfh activity.
source: This interpretation is consistent with the known role of Tregs in regulating Tfh activity (Walker, 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Tfh and Tph are subsets of human effector T cells that are closely related and have been implicated in autoimmune diseases.
source: Tfh and Tph are subsets of human effector T cells that are closely related and have been implicated in autoimmune diseases, yet have distinct phenotypes and functions, with Tfh providing help for naïve B cell differentiation and Tph acting predominantly on memory B cells (Yoshitomi and Ueno, 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about these T cell subsets supported by citation.

claim: Tfh provide help for naïve B cell differentiation and Tph act predominantly on memory B cells.
source: Tfh and Tph are subsets of human effector T cells that are closely related and have been implicated in autoimmune diseases, yet have distinct phenotypes and functions, with Tfh providing help for naïve B cell differentiation and Tph acting predominantly on memory B cells (Yoshitomi and Ueno, 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about functional differences between these subsets.

claim: Tfh are found largely in lymphoid tissues while Tph are generally found in inflamed tissues, though both seem to have a circulating component.
source: Tfh are found largely in lymphoid tissues while Tph are generally found in inflamed tissues, though both seem to have a circulating component.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the tissue distribution of these subsets.

claim: Ratios of Bcl-6 to Blimp1 transcription factors are lower for Tph than Tfh.
source: Ratios of Bcl-6 to Blimp1 transcription factors are lower for Tph than Tfh and Tph have been suggested to drive extrafollicular differentiation of age-related B cells in autoimmune disease (Yoshitomi and Ueno, 2021; Jenks et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about transcription factor expression in these subsets.

claim: Tph have been suggested to drive extrafollicular differentiation of age-related B cells in autoimmune disease.
source: Ratios of Bcl-6 to Blimp1 transcription factors are lower for Tph than Tfh and Tph have been suggested to drive extrafollicular differentiation of age-related B cells in autoimmune disease (Yoshitomi and Ueno, 2021; Jenks et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established by previous literature cited.

claim: The adoptive transfer studies are the first to suggest that there may be plasticity/interchangeability between Tfh and Tph subsets.
source: While it is unknown whether there is plasticity/interchangeability between these subsets, our adoptive transfer studies are the first, to our knowledge, to suggest that there may be.
evidence: This is a novel observation from the current study based on the phenotypic changes observed in adoptive recipients.

claim: Tph-enriched T cells showed greater proliferative capacity overall than Tfh-enriched populations from Hu/Hu and Mu/Hu mice.
source: In these studies, Tph-enriched T cells showed greater proliferative capacity overall than Tfh-enriched populations from Hu/Hu and Mu/Hu mice.
evidence: This is shown by the adoptive transfer experiments in Figure 7.

claim: The final number of Tph-like cells was quite similar and more than an order of magnitude higher than that of Tfh in recipients of either Tfh- or Tph-enriched populations.
source: Remarkably, the final number of Tph-like cells was quite similar and more than an order of magnitude higher than that of Tfh in recipients of either Tfh- or Tph-enriched populations, suggesting that Tfh may have the capacity to transition to the Tph phenotype when they expand in a lymphopenic environment.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis of adoptive recipients in Figure 7.

claim: Tfh may have the capacity to transition to the Tph phenotype when they expand in a lymphopenic environment.
source: Remarkably, the final number of Tph-like cells was quite similar and more than an order of magnitude higher than that of Tfh in recipients of either Tfh- or Tph-enriched populations, suggesting that Tfh may have the capacity to transition to the Tph phenotype when they expand in a lymphopenic environment.
evidence: This is suggested based on the phenotypic changes observed in adoptive recipients.

claim: The data directly demonstrate the pathogenicity and capacity to induce antibody secretion of expanded human Tph- and Tfh-like cells.
source: In summary, our data directly demonstrate the pathogenicity and capacity to induce antibody secretion of expanded human Tph- and Tfh-like cells and implicate both limitations in thymic selection and LIP as factors driving the development of autoimmune disease in HIS mice.
evidence: This is concluded from the adoptive transfer experiments showing disease and antibody induction.

claim: Both limitations in thymic selection and LIP are factors driving the development of autoimmune disease in HIS mice.
source: In summary, our data directly demonstrate the pathogenicity and capacity to induce antibody secretion of expanded human Tph- and Tfh-like cells and implicate both limitations in thymic selection and LIP as factors driving the development of autoimmune disease in HIS mice.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined data on thymic selection, T cell proliferation, and disease development.

claim: The observations provide a platform for the further dissection of human autoimmune disease mechanisms and therapies.
source: Since Tfh, Tph, autoantibodies, and LIP have all been implicated in various forms of human autoimmune disease, the observations here provide a platform for the further dissection of human autoimmune disease mechanisms and therapies.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential utility of the model for future research.
